title: Monitoring and related care
intro: The care that goes with gender-affirming hormone therapy: blood tests and reviews, getting the timing of a blood test right, fertility, sexual function, PrEP, and hormones around surgery. It is background reading, not a prescription. The forms each medicine comes in and the dose ranges are on the [Medicines, doses and formulations](#/doses) page.

body: Blood tests are not something you pass or fail. They tell your prescriber whether the dose is doing what you both want, and whether anything needs watching.

For feminising therapy, Australia's 2026 standards of care recommend keeping trough oestradiol above about 250 pmol/L, without a fixed upper limit, and total testosterone below 2 nmol/L for people who want full suppression [1]. The 2019 position statement suggested 250–600 pmol/L [2].

For masculinising therapy, the usual target is a trough total testosterone of about 10–20 nmol/L [1]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement and the 2020 Australian GP guides suggest 10–15 nmol/L [2][3][4]; Australia's 2026 standards of care, which this site follows, give about 10–20 [1]. Testosterone also thickens the blood, so haematocrit is checked; above about 0.50 the dose or the interval is usually reviewed [2][3]. The product information for several testosterone injections now also warns about SGLT-2 inhibitors, medicines for diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin. Taken with testosterone, they have been linked to too many red blood cells, so the blood count is checked more closely [5]. This warning is not yet in every product information, so tell your prescriber if you take one, whatever form of testosterone you use [6].
Reviews cover more than levels: blood pressure, weight, smoking, and how you are going in yourself — mood, energy, sleep, and whether the changes match what you hoped for [2][7].

Screening follows the organs you have, not your gender and not your hormones [2][7]. If you have a cervix, screening is still due every five years, and collecting your own swab is an option that many people find far easier than a speculum examination [8]. The same logic applies to breast or chest tissue, and to prostate tissue, which genital surgery does not remove [7].
list: Feminising — oestradiol and total testosterone; electrolytes and kidney function if you take spironolactone; liver function if you take cyproterone [2][3]
Masculinising — total testosterone, and a full blood count for haematocrit; liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [2][3]
Either therapy — blood pressure and weight at each review; glucose or HbA1c and lipids periodically, particularly if you have other risk factors [2][7]
Puberty blockers — bone health is monitored, because blockers pause the bone strengthening that puberty normally provides [2][7]
Before starting — baseline bloods, and a conversation about fertility and about contraception if pregnancy is possible, since neither testosterone nor oestrogen is reliable contraception [2][7]
Sexual health — STI and blood-borne virus testing as relevant to you, the same as for anyone [7]

Timing — review roughly every three months through the first year, then every six to twelve months, indefinitely [2][7]. Other guidance: Australia's 2026 standards of care suggest yearly reviews once things are stable [1]. After a change to oestrogen, levels are rechecked six to eight weeks later rather than straight away; after a change to the long-acting testosterone injection, the Equinox guide waits two more injections [3]
sections.note: Screening and monitoring are easy to lose track of when you move between services. Ask your GP to keep a written list of what is due and when, and ask for a copy yourself.

easy.text: You have blood tests before you start.
In the first year, you see your doctor about every 3 months.
After that, you go every 6 to 12 months (some guides say once a year).
If your dose changes, you have a blood test some weeks later. Your doctor tells you when.

sections.h: Getting the timing of the blood test right
body: When the sample is taken matters as much as what is measured. Most targets in the guidelines are trough levels — the lowest point, just before the next dose is due [2][3].
A sample drawn at the wrong point can look far too high or too low when nothing is wrong, and lead to a dose change you did not need.

For Testogel or testosterone cream, your prescriber will usually want the sample in the morning before you apply that day's dose [3][1]. For Testavan, it is taken 2 to 4 hours after applying [1]. For the long-acting injection, the test is booked just before the next injection is due rather than soon after one.
sections.note: Ask for the required timing to be written on your pathology form, and tell the collection centre when your last dose was. It takes ten seconds and it saves repeat tests.

sections.h: Fertility: what to know before you start
body: Hormones can lower fertility, and the loss may be permanent, although there is not enough evidence to say how often. Stopping hormones may bring fertility back, but this is not guaranteed and varies from person to person [9].
Hormones are not contraception. If a pregnancy is possible, contraception is still needed [9].
list: Storing sperm or eggs before starting hormones is an option to talk through with your prescriber [9]
It is not required: you can start hormones without storing sperm or eggs [9]
If you choose to store them, starting hormones may need to wait [9]
Storing eggs and storing sperm differ in cost and in how invasive they are [9]
Adoption is possible in Australia, but it is complex and can take careful planning [9]
sections.note: The [Trans Health SA directory](https://transhealthsa.com/directory/) lists South Australian practitioners, and its listings show which ones offer fertility services.

sections.h: Sexual function on oestrogen and blockers
body: Reduced libido, fewer spontaneous erections and reduced erectile function are recognised effects of oestrogen and androgen blockers. Some people welcome these changes; for others they cause distress [10].
Australia's 2026 standards of care describe the following options, each considered with your prescriber in light of your own goals [10].
list: Reducing the dose of oestrogen or of the androgen blocker, allowing testosterone to rise slightly; this may also bring back some masculinising effects [10]
Sildenafil or tadalafil, which improve erectile function but do not affect libido [10]
Low-dose testosterone after an orchidectomy or when testosterone is fully suppressed, with the dose guided by blood tests [10]
Low-dose testosterone cream applied to the genitals for penile pain associated with oestrogen; the standards note that this is based on clinical experience rather than research [10]
Support from a mental health professional experienced in gender-affirming care, addressing body image and the emotional aspects of sexual function [10]

body: PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is a medicine that prevents HIV. It does not interact with feminising or masculinising hormones, so the two can be taken together [11].
Australian guidelines suggest that anyone on hormones (including those with a vagina) should take PrEP every day, not only around the time of sex ("on-demand") [11].
PrEP needs regular kidney tests, HIV tests and STI checks. The kidney test matters even more if you also take spironolactone [11].

People often ask whether to stop oestrogen or testosterone before an operation, how long before, and when to restart. The question applies to any surgery, not only gender-affirming surgery: any major operation raises the risk of blood clots (venous thromboembolism) [12].

Australia's 2026 standards of care say there is not enough evidence to stop oestradiol-based therapy routinely around surgery, and that withholding gender-affirming hormones can have significant negative effects. Continuing hormones is particularly important during and after removal of the testes or ovaries (gonadectomy) [12].

Instead, the plan is individual. It weighs your risk of bleeding and of clots against the effects of going without hormones, and it is made with the surgical team. People at intermediate to high clot risk are recommended clot-prevention medicine, and whether to pause hormones is a shared decision based on your own goals [12].

Older Australian guidance differs: the 2019 position statement says oestradiol is typically stopped around the time of surgery to avoid clots, and that a blocker is not needed after an orchidectomy [2].

**Where to read more.** TransHub (ACON) has plain-language pages on each [gender-affirming surgery](https://www.transhub.org.au/trans-folk/#surgeries): facial surgery, orchidectomy, genital reconfiguration surgery, top surgery, breast implants, hysterectomy and vocal surgery. Its [genital reconfiguration surgery page](https://www.transhub.org.au/medical/grs/) notes that some surgeons ask for oestrogen to be reduced for a period before vaginoplasty, and that people with oestradiol implants may time surgery for when blood levels are low. The [Trans Health SA directory](https://transhealthsa.com/directory/) lists South Australian practitioners, including surgeons; it has no surgery information pages.
list: Tell your surgeon and your prescriber about every medicine you take, including any blocker, progesterone, testosterone injection or implant, and PrEP
For blockers, progesterone or implants, ask your surgeon and prescriber what to do around your operation
If you are told to stop a hormone, ask why, for how long, and when you can restart
Do not stop any other medicine unless your surgeon or prescriber asks you to
sections.note: Your surgeon and prescriber decide the plan for your operation together. Costs and referrals for gender-affirming surgery are on the [Resources page](#/resources).
